Agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) trains LLM agents through multi-turn interactions with external tool environments. Its multi-turn nature exposes two systems-level bottlenecks unaddressed by existing agentic RL frameworks. First, end-to-end training throughput is constrained by the slowest trajectories to complete, yet optimizing per-GPU utilization alone scatters rollout progress across many groups, delaying the completion of enough groups to unblock the next training step. Second, tool sandboxes are statically over-provisioned by their declared memory ceilings, leaving most physical memory stranded while replicating near-identical state across sandboxes launched from the same prompt. We present VenusRL, a fully disaggregated agentic RL system that addresses both bottlenecks. VenusRL’s priority-aware action scheduler uses length-prediction heuristics to identify sample groups whose completion is most likely to unblock the next training step, and pushes them ahead of others across batch admission, KV Cache residency, and cross-worker request orchestration. VenusRL’s environment resource manager combines a memory-aware admission threshold with a template-keyed page-sharing pool, packing more sandboxes per node while preserving strict memory isolation via write-protected page table entry aliasing and copy-on-write. Across representative agentic RL workloads, VenusRL achieves up to 4.24× end-to-end training speedup over state-of-the-art baselines and reduces environment cost by up to 89%. † † footnotetext: Menghao Zhang and Shuyong Zhu are the corresponding authors. 1. Introduction Agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) trains Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks through iterative interaction with external environments. Driven by this paradigm, the applications of LLMs have evolved from simple language assistants into sophisticated agents capable of solving complex, real-world problems ( Guo et al., 2025 ; OpenAI, 2022b ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025a ; Lu et al., 2025c ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . This paradigm also motivates the emergence of industry products such as Claude Code ( Anthropic, 2025 ) , OpenClaw ( Contributors, 2026 ) and Deep Research ( OpenAI, 2022b ) . Similar to conventional single-turn RL, agentic RL training is dominated by the rollout stage, which accounts for over 70% of total wall-clock time ( Qin et al., 2025a ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . Existing RL systems mainly optimize this phase by mitigating straggler-induced skewness bubbles ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Qin et al., 2025a ) . Beyond this shared characterization, the multi-turn nature of agentic trajectories introduces unique system challenges: an efficient rollout scheduling policy for maximizing end-to-end training throughput, and scalable environment interaction to support such flexible scheduling policy. First, for rollout scheduling, mainstream RL frameworks ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Contributors, 2025 ) typically adopt trajectory-level scheduling, where each trajectory is treated as an indivisible execution unit. This coarse granularity ignores generation–interaction state transitions, thereby leaving GPUs underutilized, which we call turn-level agentic bubbles . Recent works address this problem by decoupling generation controllers from environment controllers, allowing one trajectory’s generation to overlap with another’s tool interaction ( Cao et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025b ) . Though this action-level scheduling policy maximizes rollout GPU throughput, it may not accelerate training process since the trainer only waits for enough completed trajectory groups to form the next training batch, while this policy scatters rollout progress across samples. Moreover, KV Cache pressure and eviction are amplified by multi-turn execution. A trajectory may first generate, suspend during tool execution, and later resume after its KV Cache has already been evicted by other active trajectories ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Kang et al., 2026 ) . This causes repeated recomputation overhead. What’s worse, the action-level scheduling, while effective for eliminating GPU idle time, increases the number of interleaved active trajectories and thereby aggravates this problem. Both problems pose challenges for an optimized rollout scheduling policy. Second, for environment interaction, the challenge is not merely the safe execution and isolation of each tool sandboxes, but to sustain the high environment concurrency required by fine-grained rollout scheduling. Action-level scheduling increases the number of active trajectories so that rollout GPUs can consume ready trajectories while others wait for tool execution. However, if the environment side cannot support this concurrency, generation workers are blocked by interaction-side stalls, preventing action-level scheduling from fully realizing its benefit. Thus, scalable environment interaction in fact places a strong demand on high-density sandbox deployment. However, in production, sandboxes are conservatively packed by their configured memory ceilings, even though their actual resident set is far smaller, which leads to "memory stranding" ( Fuerst et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Javadi et al., 2019 ) . Worse yet, existing systems treat sandboxes as independent instances and overlook the structural property of agentic RL: a sample group consists of multiple rollouts sharing the same prompt. Therefore, trajectories within the same sample group are launched from identical templates and execute nearly identical setup code, so a fraction of their pages are byte-identical. This leads to "state duplication" ( Saxena et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) across sandboxes that could otherwise share memory. From the analysis above, we conclude an efficient agentic RL system requires two complementary capabilities: an effective rollout scheduling policy that maximizes training throughput, and a scalable environment manager that supports such scheduling policy. To the end, we propose VenusRL, a fully disaggregated system for agentic RL training. VenusRL decouples training, rollout generation, and environment interaction into independent components, and introduces two key mechanisms: a priority-aware action scheduler for end-to-end training throughput, and an environment resource manager for cost-efficient environment interaction. The priority-aware action scheduler retains the benefits of action-level scheduling by separating generation workers from environment workers. Additionally, it incorporates priority into its scheduling decisions. VenusRL defines critical groups as unfinished groups whose completion is most likely to unblock the next trainer batch. At runtime, VenusRL uses length-prediction-based heuristics to identify such groups and prioritizes their execution. To enforce this priority, VenusRL co-designs the RL framework and rollout engine to provide priority-aware GPU-slot execution, ensuring high-priority samples are scheduled ahead of others. Beyond GPU scheduling, VenusRL introduces priority-aware KV Cache residency. It employs trajectory-aware radix cache and uses a three-tier KV Cache model for admission control and eviction decisions. This preserves KV Cache entries of high-priority trajectories on a best-effort basis. Furthermore, VenusRL performs priority-aware request orchestration to mitigate the imbalanced distribution of high-priority samples across rollout workers. It monitors KV Cache pressure across rollout workers and migrates requests with their reusable prefix cache to reduce KV contention of high-priority samples. The environment resource manager provides scalable interaction by page-grained and high-density sandbox deployment. At cluster scope, VenusRL provides scalable interaction by a global controller to allocate sandboxes from a shared environment pool and hide deployment details to the framework. At node scope, VenusRL introduces page-level sandbox placement and dynamic admission control to maximize deployment density while preventing memory overcommitment. To exploit similarity among agentic trajectories, VenusRL further builds a group-level page sharing pool. Trajectories from the same sample group share snapshot pages whenever possible: read-only pages are mapped to the same write-protected physical pages, and private copies are created lazily through copy-on-write upon modification. We implemented VenusRL in 24k lines of Python, Rust and Golang. We conduct extensive evaluations to validate the effectiveness of VenusRL. Experimental data shows that VenusRL outperforms state-of-the-art RL systems, achieving 1.07–3.26 × \times end-to-end training speedup over Slime ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , 1.06-4.24 × \times speedup over RollFlash ( Lu et al., 2025b ) , and up to 2.67 × \times speedup compared to ThunderAgent ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . Meanwhile, VenusRL reduces environmental costs by up to 89% compared with E2B ( E2B Development Team, 2024 ) , a representative and widely-use sandbox platform. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions: • We identify two systems challenges introduced by agentic RL training: multi-turn rollout scheduling on the generation side, and external environment management on the interaction side (§ 2 ). • We propose VenusRL, a fully disaggregated system for Agentic RL training (§ 3 ). VenusRL introduces a priority-aware action scheduler (§ 4 ) for maximizing end-to-end training throughput, and an environment resource manager (§ 5 ) to provide scalable and cost-efficient environment interaction. • We implement VenusRL and evaluate it on representative Agentic RL workloads (§ 6 ). Experimental results show that VenusRL achieves up to 4.24 × \times training throughput improvement and reduces environment resource cost by up to 89% compared with existing systems. 2. Background and Motivation 2.1. Agentic RL Agentic RL evolves LLMs into autonomous agents capable of solving complex real-world problems, including AI coding, deep research or embodied AI ( Dou et al., 2024 ; Qi et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2022 ) . Departing from static and single-turn reasoning tasks ( OpenAI, 2022a ; Bai et al., 2024 ; Qian et al., 2025 ) , agents act through dynamic interaction with external environments. In this paradigm, LLM agents synthesize plans, invoke tools, observe feedback, and refine subsequent actions within a long-horizon execution process. A typical workflow of agentic RL training comprises three phases: rollout, reward and training. In the rollout phase, each prompt is replicated into multiple trajectories, and a rollout worker executes each trajectory by repeatedly alternating between model generation and environment interaction until reaching a terminal state. Once a trajectory is completed, a reward worker evaluates the quality of agent’s actions using a scalar reward signal. The trainer worker collects finished trajectories groups, estimates the advantage and uses them for policy optimization with algorithms like PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) or GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Agentic RL training can be performed in a synchronous or asynchronous setting. Synchronous frameworks ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Havrilla et al., 2023 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ) enforce strict on-policy training, where rollout must complete before training begins and all responses generated must use the most recent model weights. Though this synchronization stabilizes training, the system suffers from severe skewness bubble due to response variance within a single batch ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Qin et al., 2025a ) . Asynchronous frameworks ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Han et al., 2025 ) mitigate the skewness bubble by disaggregating rollout from training. However, they still fail to address the turn-level agentic bubbles caused by multi-turn interaction. 2.2. Challenges of agentic RL As quantified in previous works ( Qin et al., 2025a ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) , rollout dominates the RL training pipeline, accounting for over 70% of total wall-clock time. The rollout phase involves repeatedly transition between GPU-side LLM generation and environment-side tool execution. This iterative loop introduces two unique system challenges: multi-turn rollout pipeline scheduling on the generation side and environment resource management on the interaction side. (a) Active rollout batch size (b) KV Cache Usage & hit rate Figure 1 . Profiling results for SWE-agent task (bsz=32). Multi-turn Rollout Scheduling. Agentic trajectories alternate between GPU-side LLM generation and environment-side tool execution. Mainstream frameworks ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Contributors, 2025 ) typically schedule rollouts at the trajectory level, and are unaware of the state transitions inside each trajectory. As a result, when a trajectory pauses for tool execution, it still occupies a generation slot, leaving GPUs underutilized. We refer to this inefficiency as the turn-level agentic bubble. We profile the active generation batch size on an online SWE-agent ( Yang et al., 2024b ) workload. As shown in Figure 1(a) , although the configured generation batch size of each rollout worker is 64, the actual active batch size fluctuates substantially and reaches only 76.5% on average. To mitigate this problem, recent works ( Cao et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025b ) disaggregate environment controller from generation controller, enabling one tool execution to overlap with the other’s generation, which we call action-level scheduling policy. Though this policy successfully improves rollout GPU utilization, it may not translate into end-to-end training speedup. Since generation progress is scattered across sample groups, action-level scheduling may even delay this step’s training progress (details in § 4.1 ). Meanwhile, the multi-turn nature of agentic trajectories also introduces persistent KV Cache pressure and unexpected eviction as tokens accumulate across turns. Under limited HBM capacity, the system may be trapped in the cycle of eviction and recomputation: each trajectory generates, waits for tool execution, and later resumes after its KV Cache has been evicted by others. Figure 1(b) illustrates this severe KV thrashing. Although KV Cache usage remains constantly near saturation, the cache hit rate drops sharply and stays low, exposing substantial redundant recomputation. To mitigate this problem, hierarchical storage backends ( Qin et al., 2025b ; contributors, 2025 ) extend KV Cache capacity by offloading KV pages to lower-tier storage. However, they introduce extra reload overhead, which prior work has shown still inefficient ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Continuum ( Li et al., 2025 ) keeps KV Caches alive for a fixed time window using TTL-based management, while ThunderAgent ( Kang et al., 2026 ) evicts trajectory KV Cache with a shortest-first policy to preserve the continuity of long-context trajectories. However, these designs are still agnostic to the inner characteristics of agentic RL training. Environment Resource Management. Figure 2 . Online sandbox memory usage. Figure 3 . Non-GPU Agentic workload expenses. Agentic RL relies on external environments for tool interaction. Such interactions require strong isolation to prevent unsafe tool actions, dependency conflicts, and cross-task interference. Existing systems ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Yang et al., 2024b ; Dai et al., 2026 ) therefore commonly place each task in an isolated sandbox. Modern agentic sandboxes are deployed as microVMs ( Agache et al., 2020 ; Cloud Hypervisor Project, 2026 ) with pre-built images and fixed memory allocations. In production, memory capacity is the primary bottleneck to sandbox density (Details in Appendix A ). Unlike CPU and network resources, which can be oversubscribed with graceful performance degradation, sandbox memory is typically provisioned as a hard capacity constraint: once memory is exhausted, no additional sandboxes can be created. Prior works improve memory deployment density through execution-state reuse and resource elasticity. TrEnv ( Huang et al., 2024 ) proposes a repurposable sandbox design and facilitates remote memory state sharing by implementing a new Linux namespace API, while ARL-Tangram ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) formulates external resource management as an action-level optimization problem and dynamically allocates suitable resources to each sandbox during execution. However, none of these works fully address the following two sources of memory inefficiency for agentic sandboxes. First, to guarantee stability, production deployment therefore limits concurrency by configured peak memory rather than observed usage, introducing "memory stranding" ( Fuerst et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Javadi et al., 2019 ) . Moreover, treating each sandbox as a fully independent instance prevents reuse opportunities of shared runtimes, libraries, and dependencies, resulting in "state duplication" ( Saxena et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) . For ARL-Tangram, an additional limitation is that its elasticity relies on lightweight container-level reconfiguration and cannot be efficiently extended to strongly isolated microVM sandboxes, where resources are provisioned at the VM boundary. Our production profiling confirms this inefficiency: as shown in Figure 3 , sandbox memory usage on a physical node remains only around 8% on average, while Figure 3 shows that environment sandboxes contribute more than 60% of production non-GPU cost over the past three months. 3. VenusRL Design Overview Figure 4 . System overview and workflow of VenusRL. To address the challenges above, we propose VenusRL, a fully disaggregated system for agentic RL training, as shown in Figure 4 . Fundamentally, VenusRL follows the multi-controller paradigm adopted by prior works ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Specifically, the data coordinator serves as the centralized control plane for dataset loading, prompt preprocessing, and sample scheduling. Each rollout worker continuously fetches samples from the data coordinator using a dedicated background thread and executes generation asynchronously. When a sample group finishes generation, the rollout worker computes its advantages and streams the group to actor workers for immediate gradient computation. Once enough sample groups form a global batch, actor workers accumulate all computed gradients, and trigger a synchronized gradient computation and update across all available GPUs. The updated actor weights are then synchronized back to rollout workers before the next RL iteration. Unlike previous works ( Zhong et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) that only decouple rollout from training, VenusRL further separates environment interaction from rollout execution. Building on this architecture, VenusRL introduces two key components: a priority-aware action scheduler to maximize end-to-end training throughput, and an environment resource manager to provide scalable and cost-efficient environment interaction. Priority-aware Action Scheduler. The priority-aware action scheduler decouples generation workers from environment workers, scheduling samples at action granularity. The scheduler incorporates priority into scheduling policy, and uses a lightweight fine-tuned predictor to estimate each sample’s remaining generation length at turn boundaries for identifying high-priority sample groups. Once high-priority groups are identified, the scheduler prioritizes their samples across GPU-slot execution, KV Cache residency and runtime request orchestration. Environment Resource Manager. The environment resource manager provides scalable interaction by page-grained and high-density sandbox deployment. At cluster scope, the manager maintains a global controller that allocates sandboxes from a shared environment pool, hiding the deployment details from the RL framework. At node scope, VenusRL introduces page-level sandbox placement and dynamic admission control to maximize node deployment density while preventing memory overcommitment. Additionally, VenusRL exploits the strong similarity among agentic RL sandboxes through a group-level page pool to reuse as many as possible snapshot pages between trajectories. 4. Priority-aware Action Scheduler To mitigate the inefficiency of rollout execution discussed in § 2 , we propose priority-aware action scheduler . We begin by formalizing the optimization problem for end-to-end training. Subsequently, we propose a length-prediction heuristic to identify high-priority sample groups that contribute to end-to-end training throughput. We then design priority-aware action scheduler to prioritize high-priority samples across GPU-slot execution, KV Cache residency and request orchestration. 4.1.
